To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adversarial examples are a tiny shift of data distribution and that we can robustly train a model by sampling from the optimal distribution of adversarials.
adversarial training can be casted into a distributionally robust optimization problem and that using entropic regularization to solve it leads to faster and more robust classifiers.

(i) adversarial training can be formulated in a DRO framework with an $\infin$-Wassersten constraint and (ii) the entropic regularizer is a key ingredient to sample adversarial examples efficiently and to train robust classifiers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: how to efficiently train robust classifiers against distributional shifts of data, such as the one induced by adversarial examples?
the following two questions: (i) How to sample from the optimal adversarial distribution? (ii) How to train classifiers against this distribution?
a theoretical and empirical study of distributionally robust adversarial training with a Wasserstein constraint.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
adversarial training can be interpreted as a form of distributional robust optimization, and that this perspective can be exploited to improve the robustness of neural networks.
adversarial training is not a panacea but rather a tool to improve the generalization capabilities of neural networks.
our approach is a new way to address the problem, that is, a novel perspective, and that it outperforms existing baselines on both MNIST and CIFAR-10.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
adversarial training with the Wasserstein metric can be viewed as a distributionally robust approach to learning.
we provide a theoretical framework to robustly train classifiers against adversarial examples.
adversarial training is equivalent to distributional robustness, and that the $\infty-$ Wasserstein distance is an adequate metric to measure this distributional robustness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the adversarial training can be seen as a distributional robustness problem.
the distribution of adversarial samples can be seen as a tiny perturbation of the original data distribution and can be modeled with a DRO formulation.
the adversarial training problem is a special case of a more general distributional robust optimization problem that we can solve efficiently using optimal transport tools.
